bodies: Trade is transport. In the very fundamental basis of it, the latter is indispendable and especially in international trade where import and export of goods of many types involve considerable distances*in transportation, shipping has reigned as the supreme mode of transportation particular of voluminous amounts of goods. The increase in world trade means a corresponding demand in the shipping industry which has recently seep vast and modern developments, an inevitable consequence in the light of world trade. During the short period of about 15 years, since 1960, an important development has taken place—in the handling and transport of cargoeswith the introduction of the unitisation by containers and pallets. The traditional or conventional ‘break-bulk’ method entails the handling of different types of packing, together with the use of old-fashioned types of shore cranes or derricks on board ships. The completely new and integrated system of cargo handling has been discovered with the use of containers specially designed for dry cargo as well as liquid cargo, including specialised ‘freezer containers’ for “‘reefer’’ cargo. These containers are made of steel, aluminium alloy with plywood, wood or even plastic, but in order that the

containers can take the stress and strain of rough handling, the structure must be made from steel -or similar material, whatever the material utilised for the “outer skin’’ 2* Nations building containers have adopted the International Standards Organisation (ISO) Recommendations into their manufacturing processes and to ensure that each container is produced up to the required standard, it is ‘subjected to tests of it’s structural strength. This is_ usually done by established and reputable ship _ classification societies who are engaged in the certification of containers to ISO Specifications. _ There are varieties in the construction of con-— tainers but the ‘Standard Type’ containers manufactured have dimensions as follows: _

A purpose-built container ship has near similar characteristics of the conventional bulk carrier but the full container ship has no cranes or der- © ricks as all cargo operations are carried out by specialised wharf handling equipment. It has its engines situated aft with a compact superstruc- ~ ture of a combined poop and bridge and also with a small or no forecastle. Some container ships also have transporters or cranes able to work the full length of the vessel. _

‘TYPES OF CONTAINER SHIPS: x » There are two major types of container ships and they are the short-sea and ocean-going type. A typical short-sea container-ship is around 4000 DWT with a capacity for 148 units.of 30 footer ~ containers stowed in cellular holds and some on deck with turn-around time with fully loaded © ~ containers taking only five hours in each terminal port. The ocean-going container ship isa much =~ larger type with space for 800 units of 20 footer containers with an additional 330 refrigerated ; units. .

gures in tonnages classified into bulk crude oil, bulk dry and liquid cargo and general cargo and 75% of general cargo being containerised) it must. . be noted that movements bulk dry cargo comprise almost the same tonnages as General cargo. ~ Bulk cargo, whether liquid or dry, are not physically and economically capable‘of being containerised and are therefore more efficiently and most economically carried in specialised vessels. Such being the situation, the Bulk Cargo trade has also made tremendous progress in modern developments in the shipping industry. . BULK CARGO CARRIERS In order to cater for the increasing movements of bulk cargo, bulk vessels are being built larger and larger to meet the requirements of shipow- + ners who want to economise and reduce their operational costs. This consequentially enable shipowners to ~ offer lower freight or charter-rates to shippers. The size of bulk carriers has increased enormously as during the early sixties their average size was between 30,000 to 40,000 DWT. but increased to about 50,000—60,000 DWT: during _ the mid sixties and by the early seventies, tonnages of bulk carriers had increased up to . 100,000 DWT and above. Besides reducing operating costs, by increasing the size of vessels and the cubic capacity, the cost of building per ton decreases too. . os The development of the specialised large type of vessels for the carriage of bulk cargo has con- © tibuted in no small way to the rapid development of maritime transport or shipping. . | An increasingly large quantity of bulk cargo is being carried by speciallised or purpose-built ves; _ sels. In 1960, approximately 233 million tons of dry bulk cargo were carried by bulk carriers and merely six years later, about 340 million were carried. . An interesting point to note is that the construction of specialised bulk carriers over 15,000 dwt has made it compulsory to build specialised

Ports or ports with specialised berths and cargo handling facilities, etc. Therefore, these large vessels and specialised ports are entirely dependent _ on each other. . Andther point is that while tanker sizes increased by at least an average of 80%, bulk carriers and trampers by 52%, the general cargo liner vessels increased in sizes by only a mere 14%. Tankers and bulk carriers have benifitted and profitted from the use of very efficient wharf "facilities for loading and discharging of their cargo, but general cargo vessels are unfortunate in Bh they inherited the old-fashioned but necessary break-bulk method of loading and unloading. The problem arises because of the nature of , general cargo with its many types of commodities, irregular sizes, shapes, packings, measurements, and weights, etc. and because of their nature and characteristics, they have to be handled many times before they are stowed or unloaded in or from the vessel. Even with present facilities available at ports for general cargo liners, the car- "Mg liner part of shipping remains very labour in- » tensive and labour dependent. A likely solution _ to this is unitisation by containerisation, for as long as no pre-assembly and bulking of commodities of smaller units into larger units are done, no change of the old slow pattern is possible. ‘ _ . OIL TANKERS: The first vessel to transport oil in bulk was probably the sailing ship ‘‘Charles’’ which traded in the trans-Atlantic trade between U.S.A. and Europe. This vessel was fitted with 59 iron tanks, “each with 14 tons capacity, but since then, tankers have developed both in carrying capacity and speed, as well as the methods of construction, material and equipment used. * Modern post war tankers are from about 20,000 to 45,000 DWT, although for coastal distribution of oil, smaller tankers of 10,000 or under are in service. Tankers can also be clas-

sified by their employment, that is the type of oil they carry, which is either “clean’’ and “dirty” based on whether they carry “white oil’’ like motor spirit and kerosene or “Black oil’” such as cruide oil and fuel oil. Tankers are built with much greater strength than some cargo vessels, and they are extremely seaworthy, due to strength and greater buoyancy. It is uncommon to expect a modern tanker to get a pumping rate of over 1000 tons per hour, while larger tankers of the 30,000 class can maintain average pumping rates of between 1500/2000 tons per hour. Greater attention is also paid to the safety equipment on board tankers, due to the constant danger of fire and life boats are required to be constructed of steel or fire-resistant wood. About 50% of the world’s tankers are owned by the major oil companies and their associated companies. The other 50%:is owned by shipping companies or individuals as well as by governments as part of the fleet of their respective navies, though they are mostly chartered to oil companies to supplement their fleet. Tankers are at present transporting half of the world’s seaborne trade. It has been found profitable to build super or mammoth tankers to effect real economies. The average tonnage of the biggest oil tankers is over 150,000 DWT as a tonmile for a 200,000 Dwt tanker is only half of that of a tanker of 50,000 Dwt. However the cost of operations still decreases per ton-mile up to over 230,000 Dwt but after the decrease rate shows a gradual decline. Over the last twenty years, the shipping industry has seen tremendous developments and this period is considered: a very remarkable phase in the history of shipping and the changes made almost entirely altered the former pattern of cargo handling methods, port facilities and especially the type of ships, which has become larger and more specialised.

06bf5374-4b8f-4f19-ac8c-6d5ad6de7890.title: THE SUEZ SURCHARGE AMENDMENT
bodies: During the period from mid-December till the end of March, Lines of the Far Eastern Freight Conference (FEFC) are engaged in a gradual rescheduling via the Suez Canal of their larger container vessels, which have hitherto been routed via the Cape of Good Hope or the Panama Canal. During the phasing-in period, the Lines have been examining the effect of the Suez Routing ‘on the current Suez Surcharge, taking all factors into consideration, the findings being carried out by an international firm of independent accountants. Through the findings, the FEFC has reached a decision to reduce the Suez Canal surcharge from 4.75 perceht to 2 percent with effect from April 1. Mr. W.J.V. Cook, FEFC Representative for Malaysia and Singapore said that the findings show that though the cost of transiting Suez for _ a convéntional vessel has increased somewhat more than the freight rate increases introduced. between the closing of the Canal in 1967, its re-opening in 1975 and today, the increase is fairly small and the Lines have agreed to ignore the increase. = However, in the case of container vessels, partly because of higher Suez Canal dues and partly due to higher costs in respect of operations for transiting the Canal, the total cost per bill-of lading ton (1,000 kilos or one cubic metre) of cargo is in excess of that for conventional vessels. A review of the FEFC Annual Report for 1975 revealed that the closure of the Canal of 1967 presented the FEFC Lines with immediate problems — the first being that several of their ships were trapped there and of even more importance, is the fact the enforced change of route round the Cape of Good Hope added something like 3,500 nautical miles to a one-way voyage from the Far East and thus there was a sudden requirement for extra tonnage. This meant that building programmes and plans for fleet expansion had to be radically reviewed in the light of the possibility that the Canal might remain closed for some time or. even permanently. At the same time, the Lines had to meet the extra costs of fuel, crews, dePreciation and maintenance, all of which rose sharply with the longer voyage time, At that time, a ‘Suez surcharge’ of 10 percent was introduced to help meet the increased costs which was later stablised at a figure of 7.5 percent. This incorporated into the basic freight rate and maintained until the Canal was reopened in 1975. The reopening of the Canal brought about expectations that the FEFC would be able to reduce or abolish the Suez surcharge, since there was no necessity for any ships to take the longer route via the Cape. The position was not, however as simple as appeared. In the first place, during the course, the Lines had introduced containerships or semicontainerships into service and the largest of these vessels are equivalent in capacity to several conventional ships and some were quite simply too big to transit the Canal when it reopened. Secondly, these newer vessels are very much faster than the older conventional ships so that the time to be saved by using the Suez Canal instead of the Cape route was less important than it was before. Nevertheless, with the gradual increase in the number of Lines’ vessels using the waterway,

several reductions have been made to the surcharge. In June 1975, the figure was reduced from 7.5 percent to 6 percent and a further reduction, to 5.25 was made in October 1976. A third reduction to 4.75, took effect in February the same year and the FEFC had kept the position under review. In November 1975, the FEFC stated that in fonfirmity with requests from shippers’ councils the Suez surcharge would be separated from the base rate and reapplied as a separate surcharge. Accounting for the level of surcharge was that continue on page 4 =~

although transit via the Canal results in a saving in fuel, certain other costs have increased, notab- ly Canal dues which are considerably higher than the 1976 level and special insurance. Further- more after the reopening, the size of the largest containerships gave rise to certain navigational problems as owners of such large and valuable vessels naturally wished to be wholly satisfied in all respects of the feasibility of frequent and regular transits via the Canal. Since June 1975, discussions have taken place with the Suez Canal Authority on all aspects of the use of the Canal and the recent findings show that the excess cost, averaged over container and conventional vessels warrants a retention of art of the Suez surcharge slightly in excess of 2 percent and in the light of this, the Lines have ultimately decided to reduce the present surcharge of 4.75 percent to 2 percent, with effect from Apr. 1 1977. Mr. Cook in conclusion said that with the reduction in the surcharge on April 1, a compensatory revision of the Bunder Adjustment Factor (BAF) will be made, based on the monthly review of the BAF formula in March. The Baf will then continue to be reviewed monthly for bunker prices as hitherto. 3 Meanwhile, the Singapore and Malaysian National Shippers’ Councils and the Federation of Asean Shippers’ Councils (FSC) have been informed of the FEFC reduction of the Suez surcharge and supplied with the report of the accountants.

6711b282-fe02-441c-9626-4bfa8045efd7.title: A NEW GEOPHYSICAL COMPANY | FORMED
bodies: The first company in Britian, to operate a commercial hydrographic survey department, Kelvin Hughes has joined forces with Compagnie Generale de Geophysique, the largest geophysical company in Europe and one of the largest in the world, to form Anglo-French Offshore Surveys Limited. Chairman of the new company, Mr. Peter Prior who is also Director and General Manager of Kelvin Hughes said, ‘The merger will bring about the pooling of our geophysical, positioning and hydrographic resources. This will enable us | to offer a comprehensive survey service which is unique in its scope.’ Anglo-French Offshore Surveys Until use both manual and computerised facilities including the most modern computerised data processing. Although the Headquarters of the new company is sited in London, its facilities and expertise will be available throughout the world through the subsidiaries of its parent companies, including Kelvin Hughes in Singapore and Malaysia.

74073a28-6d41-4821-ab38-67db4a0fca32.title: BY 1978~THE SINGAPORE | MARITIME CENTRE (SMC)
bodies: The main approach to the building is via the ground floor which has also been planned to accommodate shops and a terminal concourse. The terminal concourse at the seaward side of the ground floor rises through a height of 4.6 m. There will be a mooring structure for berthing ocean going liners and facilities to clear passengers. The terminal concourse will also provide a central position for a tourist information counter and travel agencies, to serve the needs of tourists and passengers passing through the terminal. At the west wing, there will be a two-storey structure for a covered ferry terminal and a concourse for commuters and to complement the ferry service, a taxi terminal is also expected to be located here. On the mezzanine floor and first floor, will be a well-facilitated exhibition hall, supported by ancilliary services provided by shops with an extensive and specialised selection of merchandise on both floors. On the second floor too, will be an exclusive super departmental store allowing a free flow of shoppers within one store. Parking space for some 1,070 cars will be provided from the 3rd to 7th floor. Two ramps constructed at each side of the building facilitates the smooth flow of traffic between the storeyed car-parks and the runways on the ground floor. A discotheque is planned on the third floor which will provide a splendid view of Keppel Harbour. From the 8th to 9th floor, the Singapore Maritime Centre will house an efficiently coordinated congregation of import and export enterprises, banks, transportation services, insurance companies, trade and commercial organisations, as well as government, statutory and other public offices closely affiliated to world trade. This layout will no doubt bea great boost to the clearance of trade documents under one roof. Situated on the 10th floor will bea luxurious theatre-restaurant, a 44-lane bowling alley which will be the largest in sifedbere in terms of number lanes occupying a single stretch of space and the remaining area will be taken up by office modules. Last but not least is the roof level housing the World Trade Centre Club, Singapore, with facilities planned exclusively to provide a social setting for the Singapore world traders, businessmen and professionals. There will be a well-equipped multi-purpose hall and some 20 dayrooms for visitors from overseas and members will have access to facilities of a health club, squash courts and other club amenities. When the building eventually houses the World Trade Centre, Singapore, business and commercial communities will have access to a computerized international commercial date system which is part of the comprehensive information system essential for efficient international business transactions.

It will tremendously augment and complement Singapore's capacity as the hub of the regions’ trade and it will be, in itself, Singapore’s biggest single contribution to facilities and services required by businessmen for the promotion of international trade in a more efficient and effective manner. The Singapore Maritime Centre (SMC), a S$83 million, 12-storey building complex which will be completed in early 1978, is a project developed by the Port of Singapore Authority. With this project, a unique blend of commercial, recreational and maritime terminal facilities the PSA envisages a global trade service for the manufacturer or trader, incorporating the most upto-date facilities designed to expedite the development and operation of an effective international trade system. Situated at the western extremity of Keppel Wharves at Jardine Steps, a rapidly developing area just at the outskirt of the Central Business District, the SMC is strategically close to port administration and facilities of the Port of Singapore Authority and therefore has the full advantages as a marine terminal for ocean-going liners/ cruises and ferry services to holiday resorts in the Southern Islands and neighbouring region. A definitely prominent landmark at Jardine Steps, the T-shaped building (230 x 130m) covering a site of 3.3 ha of which about 0.8 ha will be over the sea,will also be one of the largest building in Singapore in terms of floor area — its floor area covers 144,000 sq. m.

The main approach to the building is via the ground floor which has also been planned to accommodate shops and a terminal concourse. The terminal concourse at the seaward side of the ground floor rises through a height of 4.6 m. There will be a mooring structure for berthing ocean going liners and facilities to clear passengers. The terminal concourse will also provide a central position for a tourist information counter and travel agencies, to serve the needs of tourists and passengers passing through the terminal. At the west wing, there will be a two-storey structure for a covered ferry terminal and a concourse for commuters and to complement the ferry service, a taxi terminal is also expected to be located here. On the mezzanine floor and first floor, will be a well-facilitated exhibition hall, supported by ancilliary services provided by shops with an extensive and specialised selection of merchandise on both floors. On the second floor too, will be an exclusive super departmental store allowing a free flow of shoppers within one store. Parking space for some 1,070 cars will be provided from the 3rd to 7th floor. Two ramps constructed at each side of the building facilitates the smooth flow of traffic between the storeyed car-parks and the runways on the ground floor. A discotheque is planned on the third floor which will provide a splendid view of Keppel Harbour. From the 8th to 9th floor, the Singapore Maritime Centre will house an efficiently co-

ordinated congregation of import and export enterprises, banks, transportation services, insurance companies, trade and commercial organisations, as well as government, statutory and other public offices closely affiliated to world trade. This layout will no doubt bea great boost to the clearance of trade documents under one roof. Situated on the 10th floor will bea luxurious theatre-restaurant, a 44-lane bowling alley which will be the largest in sifedbere in terms of number lanes occupying a single stretch of space and the remaining area will be taken up by office modules. Last but not least is the roof level housing the World Trade Centre Club, Singapore, with facilities planned exclusively to provide a social setting for the Singapore world traders, businessmen and professionals. There will be a well-equipped multi-purpose hall and some 20 dayrooms for visitors from overseas and members will have access to facilities of a health club, squash courts and other club amenities. When the building eventually houses the World Trade Centre, Singapore, business and commercial communities will have access to a computerized international commercial date system which is part of the comprehensive information system essential for efficient international business transactions.
MODERN DEVELOPMENT IN THE SHIPPING INDUSTRIES ~1960 TO PRESENT °2:5-/22%..
S. L. KOONG

Trade is transport. In the very fundamental basis of it, the latter is indispendable and especially in international trade where import and export of goods of many types involve considerable distances*in transportation, shipping has reigned as the supreme mode of transportation particular of voluminous amounts of goods. The increase in world trade means a corresponding demand in the shipping industry which has recently seep vast and modern developments, an inevitable consequence in the light of world trade. During the short period of about 15 years, since 1960, an important development has taken place—in the handling and transport of cargoeswith the introduction of the unitisation by containers and pallets. The traditional or conventional ‘break-bulk’ method entails the handling of different types of packing, together with the use of old-fashioned types of shore cranes or derricks on board ships. The completely new and integrated system of cargo handling has been discovered with the use of containers specially designed for dry cargo as well as liquid cargo, including specialised ‘freezer containers’ for “‘reefer’’ cargo. These containers are made of steel, aluminium alloy with plywood, wood or even plastic, but in order that the

containers can take the stress and strain of rough handling, the structure must be made from steel -or similar material, whatever the material utilised for the “outer skin’’ 2* Nations building containers have adopted the International Standards Organisation (ISO) Recommendations into their manufacturing processes and to ensure that each container is produced up to the required standard, it is ‘subjected to tests of it’s structural strength. This is_ usually done by established and reputable ship _ classification societies who are engaged in the certification of containers to ISO Specifications. _ There are varieties in the construction of con-— tainers but the ‘Standard Type’ containers manufactured have dimensions as follows: _

~~ During this period of-transition'from conven- ~ tional type ‘ships to special-built cellular hold ships, there is the necessity to adapt to the modern mode of cargo handling and transportation . and some vessels are being converted into semicontainer-ships to maximise on their operational efficiency.

A purpose-built container ship has near similar characteristics of the conventional bulk carrier but the full container ship has no cranes or der- © ricks as all cargo operations are carried out by specialised wharf handling equipment. It has its engines situated aft with a compact superstruc- ~ ture of a combined poop and bridge and also with a small or no forecastle. Some container ships also have transporters or cranes able to work the full length of the vessel. _

‘TYPES OF CONTAINER SHIPS: x » There are two major types of container ships and they are the short-sea and ocean-going type. A typical short-sea container-ship is around 4000 DWT with a capacity for 148 units.of 30 footer ~ containers stowed in cellular holds and some on deck with turn-around time with fully loaded © ~ containers taking only five hours in each terminal port. The ocean-going container ship isa much =~ larger type with space for 800 units of 20 footer containers with an additional 330 refrigerated ; units. .
TYPES OF CARGO SUITABLE FOR - , : » CONTAINERS Although the impact of containerisation is tremendous and justifiably so (World Trade fi-

gures in tonnages classified into bulk crude oil, bulk dry and liquid cargo and general cargo and 75% of general cargo being containerised) it must. . be noted that movements bulk dry cargo comprise almost the same tonnages as General cargo. ~ Bulk cargo, whether liquid or dry, are not physically and economically capable‘of being containerised and are therefore more efficiently and most economically carried in specialised vessels. Such being the situation, the Bulk Cargo trade has also made tremendous progress in modern developments in the shipping industry. . BULK CARGO CARRIERS In order to cater for the increasing movements of bulk cargo, bulk vessels are being built larger and larger to meet the requirements of shipow- + ners who want to economise and reduce their operational costs. This consequentially enable shipowners to ~ offer lower freight or charter-rates to shippers. The size of bulk carriers has increased enormously as during the early sixties their average size was between 30,000 to 40,000 DWT. but increased to about 50,000—60,000 DWT: during _ the mid sixties and by the early seventies, tonnages of bulk carriers had increased up to . 100,000 DWT and above. Besides reducing operating costs, by increasing the size of vessels and the cubic capacity, the cost of building per ton decreases too. . os The development of the specialised large type of vessels for the carriage of bulk cargo has con- © tibuted in no small way to the rapid development of maritime transport or shipping. . | An increasingly large quantity of bulk cargo is being carried by speciallised or purpose-built ves; _ sels. In 1960, approximately 233 million tons of dry bulk cargo were carried by bulk carriers and merely six years later, about 340 million were carried. . An interesting point to note is that the construction of specialised bulk carriers over 15,000 dwt has made it compulsory to build specialised

Ports or ports with specialised berths and cargo handling facilities, etc. Therefore, these large vessels and specialised ports are entirely dependent _ on each other. . Andther point is that while tanker sizes increased by at least an average of 80%, bulk carriers and trampers by 52%, the general cargo liner vessels increased in sizes by only a mere 14%. Tankers and bulk carriers have benifitted and profitted from the use of very efficient wharf "facilities for loading and discharging of their cargo, but general cargo vessels are unfortunate in Bh they inherited the old-fashioned but necessary break-bulk method of loading and unloading. The problem arises because of the nature of , general cargo with its many types of commodities, irregular sizes, shapes, packings, measurements, and weights, etc. and because of their nature and characteristics, they have to be handled many times before they are stowed or unloaded in or from the vessel. Even with present facilities available at ports for general cargo liners, the car- "Mg liner part of shipping remains very labour in- » tensive and labour dependent. A likely solution _ to this is unitisation by containerisation, for as long as no pre-assembly and bulking of commodities of smaller units into larger units are done, no change of the old slow pattern is possible. ‘ _ . OIL TANKERS: The first vessel to transport oil in bulk was probably the sailing ship ‘‘Charles’’ which traded in the trans-Atlantic trade between U.S.A. and Europe. This vessel was fitted with 59 iron tanks, “each with 14 tons capacity, but since then, tankers have developed both in carrying capacity and speed, as well as the methods of construction, material and equipment used. * Modern post war tankers are from about 20,000 to 45,000 DWT, although for coastal distribution of oil, smaller tankers of 10,000 or under are in service. Tankers can also be clas-

sified by their employment, that is the type of oil they carry, which is either “clean’’ and “dirty” based on whether they carry “white oil’’ like motor spirit and kerosene or “Black oil’” such as cruide oil and fuel oil. Tankers are built with much greater strength than some cargo vessels, and they are extremely seaworthy, due to strength and greater buoyancy. It is uncommon to expect a modern tanker to get a pumping rate of over 1000 tons per hour, while larger tankers of the 30,000 class can maintain average pumping rates of between 1500/2000 tons per hour. Greater attention is also paid to the safety equipment on board tankers, due to the constant danger of fire and life boats are required to be constructed of steel or fire-resistant wood. About 50% of the world’s tankers are owned by the major oil companies and their associated companies. The other 50%:is owned by shipping companies or individuals as well as by governments as part of the fleet of their respective navies, though they are mostly chartered to oil companies to supplement their fleet. Tankers are at present transporting half of the world’s seaborne trade. It has been found profitable to build super or mammoth tankers to effect real economies. The average tonnage of the biggest oil tankers is over 150,000 DWT as a tonmile for a 200,000 Dwt tanker is only half of that of a tanker of 50,000 Dwt. However the cost of operations still decreases per ton-mile up to over 230,000 Dwt but after the decrease rate shows a gradual decline. Over the last twenty years, the shipping industry has seen tremendous developments and this period is considered: a very remarkable phase in the history of shipping and the changes made almost entirely altered the former pattern of cargo handling methods, port facilities and especially the type of ships, which has become larger and more specialised.

The drydock, a £162-million drydock and ship repait complex built for the Dubai Dry* Sa = dock Company, has seen its first stage of completion — the pumping of about 370 million gallons of seawater from two of its docks and the working area inside a temporary cofferdam. - » Done in four stages, the operation rerequired fourteen electric submersible 4 pumps which kept the area dry so the next stage of construction can be carried out. The third and smallest dock will be ‘dewatered’ when the dock walls are completed and the cofferdam is extended. Meanwhile, the completion of the first stage of pumping will enable the dock floors and sills to be concreted and the dock gates to be installed. _ Situated at Dubai, in the United Arab Emirates, the multi-million dock is being built by contractors, Costain-Taylor Woodrow Joint Venture, under the direction of ‘ consulting engineers, Sir William Halcrow » and Partners. “ SR RES URES EEE Sea, SERRE
THE SUEZ SURCHARGE AMENDMENT

During the period from mid-December till the end of March, Lines of the Far Eastern Freight Conference (FEFC) are engaged in a gradual rescheduling via the Suez Canal of their larger container vessels, which have hitherto been routed via the Cape of Good Hope or the Panama Canal. During the phasing-in period, the Lines have been examining the effect of the Suez Routing ‘on the current Suez Surcharge, taking all factors into consideration, the findings being carried out by an international firm of independent accountants. Through the findings, the FEFC has reached a decision to reduce the Suez Canal surcharge from 4.75 perceht to 2 percent with effect from April 1. Mr. W.J.V. Cook, FEFC Representative for Malaysia and Singapore said that the findings show that though the cost of transiting Suez for _ a convéntional vessel has increased somewhat more than the freight rate increases introduced. between the closing of the Canal in 1967, its re-opening in 1975 and today, the increase is fairly small and the Lines have agreed to ignore the increase. = However, in the case of container vessels, partly because of higher Suez Canal dues and partly due to higher costs in respect of operations for transiting the Canal, the total cost per bill-of lading ton (1,000 kilos or one cubic metre) of cargo is in excess of that for conventional vessels. A review of the FEFC Annual Report for 1975 revealed that the closure of the Canal of 1967 presented the FEFC Lines with immediate problems — the first being that several of their ships were trapped there and of even more importance, is the fact the enforced change of route round the Cape of Good Hope added something like 3,500 nautical miles to a one-way voyage from the Far East and thus there was a sudden requirement for extra tonnage. This meant that building programmes and plans for fleet expansion had to be radically reviewed in the light of the possibility that the Canal might remain closed for some time or. even permanently. At the same time, the Lines had to meet the extra costs of fuel, crews, dePreciation and maintenance, all of which rose sharply with the longer voyage time, At that time, a ‘Suez surcharge’ of 10 percent was introduced to help meet the increased costs which was later stablised at a figure of 7.5 percent. This incorporated into the basic freight rate and maintained until the Canal was reopened in 1975. The reopening of the Canal brought about expectations that the FEFC would be able to reduce or abolish the Suez surcharge, since there was no necessity for any ships to take the longer route via the Cape. The position was not, however as simple as appeared. In the first place, during the course, the Lines had introduced containerships or semicontainerships into service and the largest of these vessels are equivalent in capacity to several conventional ships and some were quite simply too big to transit the Canal when it reopened. Secondly, these newer vessels are very much faster than the older conventional ships so that the time to be saved by using the Suez Canal instead of the Cape route was less important than it was before. Nevertheless, with the gradual increase in the number of Lines’ vessels using the waterway,

several reductions have been made to the surcharge. In June 1975, the figure was reduced from 7.5 percent to 6 percent and a further reduction, to 5.25 was made in October 1976. A third reduction to 4.75, took effect in February the same year and the FEFC had kept the position under review. In November 1975, the FEFC stated that in fonfirmity with requests from shippers’ councils the Suez surcharge would be separated from the base rate and reapplied as a separate surcharge. Accounting for the level of surcharge was that continue on page 4 =~

although transit via the Canal results in a saving in fuel, certain other costs have increased, notab- ly Canal dues which are considerably higher than the 1976 level and special insurance. Further- more after the reopening, the size of the largest containerships gave rise to certain navigational problems as owners of such large and valuable vessels naturally wished to be wholly satisfied in all respects of the feasibility of frequent and regular transits via the Canal. Since June 1975, discussions have taken place with the Suez Canal Authority on all aspects of the use of the Canal and the recent findings show that the excess cost, averaged over container and conventional vessels warrants a retention of art of the Suez surcharge slightly in excess of 2 percent and in the light of this, the Lines have ultimately decided to reduce the present surcharge of 4.75 percent to 2 percent, with effect from Apr. 1 1977. Mr. Cook in conclusion said that with the reduction in the surcharge on April 1, a compensatory revision of the Bunder Adjustment Factor (BAF) will be made, based on the monthly review of the BAF formula in March. The Baf will then continue to be reviewed monthly for bunker prices as hitherto. 3 Meanwhile, the Singapore and Malaysian National Shippers’ Councils and the Federation of Asean Shippers’ Councils (FSC) have been informed of the FEFC reduction of the Suez surcharge and supplied with the report of the accountants.

A NEW ; GEOPHYSICAL COMPANY | FORMED

The first company in Britian, to operate a commercial hydrographic survey department, Kelvin Hughes has joined forces with Compagnie Generale de Geophysique, the largest geophysical company in Europe and one of the largest in the world, to form Anglo-French Offshore Surveys Limited. Chairman of the new company, Mr. Peter Prior who is also Director and General Manager of Kelvin Hughes said, ‘The merger will bring about the pooling of our geophysical, positioning and hydrographic resources. This will enable us | to offer a comprehensive survey service which is unique in its scope.’ Anglo-French Offshore Surveys Until use both manual and computerised facilities including the most modern computerised data processing. Although the Headquarters of the new company is sited in London, its facilities and expertise will be available throughout the world through the subsidiaries of its parent companies, including Kelvin Hughes in Singapore and Malaysia.
